verdicts.quote: I’d prefer structured fields—nurses already enter vitals, medications, and key observations in the handover sheet, so we should capture those consistently. The form will include fields for blood pressure, heart rate, temperature, pain score, and any new medications, with dropdowns or numeric inputs where possible. Nurses can still add free text at the end for context

No, GDPR and our hospital’s data governance policy are sufficient—I don’t need anything extra. But I do want to make sure the tool logs every time a note is created or edited, and who did it, so we can audit access later. ... The logs will include the nurse’s ID, timestamp, and action type—like “created” or “edited”—and will be retained for at least seven years
The first thing a nurse does when they start a shift is open the tool from their tablet, log in with their NHS smartcard
They select the patient they’re responsible for—usually by tapping their name or MRN—and the tool auto-populates the patient’s bed number and current status

They need to see the dose, the unit (like mg or mL), and the time the medication was given—those three details are critical. The tool should show them a dropdown with the approved medications from the hospital’s formulary, so they can’t type free text and risk errors. If they enter a new medication, it should be flagged for review by the ward manager the next day. They also need to confirm the patient’s bed number and MRN are correct before saving—those are auto-filled from Epic but must be visible for double-checking
The audit log will keep every version of a note with its timestamp and author, so the history of a change like 8 to 4 can always be traced. ... The log is stored read-only for seven years

The ward manager will use it once per shift to review the notes before handover—they’ll open the tool, check the list of completed notes, and look for any gaps or inconsistencies. ... The ward manager's list will include medication flags for new entries, so they can review them the next day

Letting nurses enter observations first—those are the most frequent and time-sensitive updates, especially blood pressure and heart rate, which need to be recorded at the start of each shift. The pain score is also critical for patient care and often missed during retyping. ... The form includes clear fields for each observation, with dropdowns or numeric inputs

Yes, keep the default—heart rates above 200 should trigger a warning, as they’re extremely rare and likely a typo. I’ll also set a limit for temperature: anything above 45°C or below 30°C should show a warning. For blood pressure, systolic above 250 or below 80, and diastolic above 150 or below 50, should be flagged. ... a warning will help catch input errors without stopping the nurse

I’d say block the save—this is a critical field that affects patient care, and we can’t risk it being skipped. The system should show a clear message: “Pain score is missing—please enter a value before saving.”
I’ll make sure the form includes clear fields for each observation, with dropdowns or numeric inputs to reduce errors

I’d say show a warning, not block it—some medications have variable dosing based on weight or condition, and a high dose might be correct for a specific patient. But the warning should be clear: “This dose is 10 times the usual amount—please confirm with a senior nurse or pharmacist.” That gives the nurse a chance to double-check without stopping the workflow

Before saving, the nurse must see the dose, unit (like mg or mL), and time given clearly displayed in the form—each in its own labeled field, not hidden in a note. The time should default to the current time, but they should be able to edit it if it’s wrong. The unit must be selected from a dropdown, not typed free text

verdicts.quote: The author can view their own edit history. - The charge nurse can view the edit history. - The original content is preserved in the audit trail. - Every edit creates a new version in Azure SQL with VersionId, PreviousContent, EditTimestamp, and EditorId. - The charge nurse can view the edit history via a dropdown in the UI. - The spreadsheet reflects only the latest version. - View History lists all versions with timestamp, editor ID and content - Versions are sorted chronologically and the latest version is highlighted

The “Pending Action” tag is replaced with “Escalated” when a charge nurse updates the note status. The original tag is preserved in the audit log along with the timestamp and the user ID of the charge nurse who made the change.

The charge nurse can re-escalate the note if the original author does not resolve it within 24 hours of escalation. The system will track the escalation timestamp and trigger a reminder via Azure Logic Apps if no resolution occurs.

The system should display a client-side validation error: “Patient must be selected before saving.” This message appears inline beneath the patient selection dropdown with a red border and icon. The save button is disabled until a valid patient is selected.

The spreadsheet and the charge nurse’s UI dropdown will always display the latest version of the note content, with the version history stored in the JSON field but only accessible via an explicit “View History” button.

The spreadsheet will show the updated content from the 08:00 edit, as the sync at 08:15 pulls the latest version from Azure SQL. If the author opens “View History” afterward, they will see a list of all versions.

verdicts.quote: A nurse documented a patient’s fall risk assessment during evening rounds. She first entered the note into the EPR using the FHIR Observation resource: fields included patient ID, timestamp, author (her NHS ID), category (clinical assessment), code (‘fall-risk’), and text

After login, senior nurse sees only pending notes for selected ward - Notes with blank author IDs or failed syncs do not appear in nurse dashboard

Pending means notes that have been created in the EPR but not yet acknowledged by a senior nurse or clinical lead—specifically, any FHIR Observation with a “note status” of “pending review” and a non-blank author ID

The ward selection is dynamic and can be changed mid-shift. When a nurse switches wards, she selects the new ward from the same dropdown, and the system immediately reloads the patient list and pending notes for that ward. The change is reflected instantly, with no need to log out or restart. However, the system logs the ward switch in the audit trail with the NHS ID and timestamp, and retains the old ward context for 30 minutes to support reconciliation

When a Band 5 nurse acknowledges a note, the system records the NHS ID of the nurse, the timestamp (UTC), and the action type ("acknowledged") as a FHIR Annotation resource linked to the original Observation. This annotation is visible to all senior nurses, clinical leads, and ward clerks with read access. The acknowledgment is not editable or deletable

A nurse can edit a saved note within 15 minutes of submission—after that, the note becomes immutable. When edited, the system creates a new FHIR Observation resource with the corrected data, marks the original as “replaced,” and adds a FHIR Annotation stating “Version 2: corrected patient ID.” All changes are logged in the audit trail with the NHS ID, timestamp, and action

When a nurse successfully saves a note, the UI displays a green confirmation toast with the message “Note saved and synced to EPR,” followed by a timestamp in UTC. The note immediately appears in the patient’s note list with the author’s name and the “saved” status, and the “Save” button changes to “Saved” with a checkmark icon. Additionally, the audit log captures the event with the action type “created,” NHS ID, and timestamp
A failed EPR write returns an error to the nurse, and the note stays in draft

verdicts.quote: Hospital IT administrators need access to the tool’s health monitoring dashboard—available via Azure Monitor and Application Insights—to track API latency, error rates, and authentication failures.

The primary user is the ward nurse, who needs to log in via Azure AD SSO, select a patient from their assigned shift roster (pulled from the ward scheduling API), and enter a free-text clinical note using a clean, mobile-responsive form that auto-saves every 30 seconds.

If Epic is unreachable during submission, the note is immediately persisted to our Azure SQL Database with a status of “Pending” and a retry queue is triggered via Azure Service Bus. The system automatically retries the FHIR POST every 30 seconds for up to 15 minutes...

Additionally, a pharmacy liaison may need read-only access to the note feed for specific alerts (e.g., “patient refusing medication”) to initiate interventions, but only with explicit approval and audit logging.

Only the pharmacy liaison and the charge nurse can open an alert-flagged note, and each access is logged in Azure Monitor with the user ID, timestamp, IP address, and the note’s MRN. When the liaison opens the note, they must select a reason from a dropdown...

When a nurse submits a note with the alert type “Patient refusing medication,” ... The liaison can click to open it, which triggers an automated workflow: a Microsoft Teams message is sent to the pharmacy team channel with a link to the note, and a ticket is created in our incident tracking system (ServiceNow) with priority level 2.

At the end of their shift, the ward nurse can access a “Shift Summary” view that shows all notes they submitted during the shift, with color-coded status: green for “Synced to Epic,” yellow for “Pending retry,” and red for “Failed after 15 minutes.” They can tap any failed note to see the error message and retry it manually if desired.

At the start of their shift, the charge nurse opens the dashboard and sees a real-time summary of all ward notes from the prior shift: a list of patients with active notes, color-coded by status—green for “synced,” yellow for “pending,” and red for “failed.” They immediately see any alert-flagged notes ... The system auto-refreshes every 2 minutes during the shift.

While waiting to retry, the nurse sees a persistent notification at the top of the screen: “Your note is pending sync—will retry automatically. Status: Retry attempt #2 (30 seconds ago).” The retry status updates every 30 seconds with a progress graphic.

The charge nurse dashboard displays a real-time summary of all ward notes from the prior shift. The dashboard shows a list of patients with active notes color-coded by status. The dashboard displays alert-flagged notes in a dedicated section with a red badge. The dashboard shows a count of unresolved issues. The dashboard auto-refreshes every 2 minutes during the shift. The charge nurse can view the full note history per patient. The charge nurse can export the overview to PDF for handoff.

The PDF handoff is shared with the incoming charge nurse and the unit manager, who receive it via secure email through Azure Logic Apps, with encryption and a 7-day expiration link. The export is logged in the audit trail with the user ID, timestamp, patient count, and recipient email, and stored in Azure Blob Storage with a 7-year retention policy—exactly like alert-note access.

If the note fails after 15 minutes, the system triggers a push notification (via Azure Notification Hub) and displays a modal: “Note saved locally—sync failed due to Epic outage. Contact IT if issue persists.” The message remains visible until acknowledged, ensuring no note is silently lost—this is logged as a failed write event in Azure Monitor, visible to the IT team.

When a nurse opens the app, they must be able to authenticate via Azure AD SSO and immediately see their assigned shift roster—displayed as a list of patient cards—with real-time status indicators ... This data must load within 3 seconds, and the nurse must be able to click any patient card to begin note entry—even if the network is slow, with all patient data cached locally for up to 5 minutes.

The nurse sees the status from the ward shift system—the bed is empty—so the card shows “Bed Empty” and is dimmed, with a small tooltip: “Patient transferred per ward system; note may not be relevant.” The card does not display the Epic admission status of “Transfer” in this case, because the shift system’s real-time bed state takes precedence.

If the nurse attempts to enter a note for that patient, a modal appears: “Patient not assigned to this ward—note will not sync to Epic. Confirm continue?” This prevents invalid data entry and maintains data integrity.

The test must verify that the roster drops the patient within 60 seconds of the ward shift system updating their status—specifically, the system must detect the change via the REST API polling interval (set to 30 seconds) and refresh the roster within 90 seconds of the update.
The patient card is removed within 90 seconds of the shift system update.

Yes, version one must support full offline note creation and editing—nurses must be able to start typing a note, save it locally, and edit it later even if the device loses network connectivity. The app uses IndexedDB for local persistence, a service worker to cache assets and handle offline state, and a conflict resolution strategy that prioritizes the latest version based on timestamp when sync succeeds.
Only patients assigned to the nurse's current ward per the ward shift system appear; Epic-only admissions do not appear. Discrepancies between systems are logged with timestamps from both sources.
